rationale: No panel dissent is attached, and the ledger is the same twelve weak records from one unverified source that the incumbent weighed. The case verdict (unresolved), the load-bearing set, the headers, the featured set of twenty-four and the crux order all stand. One per-claim grade is corrected, which is why a complete assessment is returned: DEEP-C009 (Jiroft handle wear) was carried as weakly supported, but its only evidence record, DEEP-E023, is a context record — the page points to the Vidale and Micheli wear-trace study; the study's finding is not in the ledger — and the incumbent's own prose conceded the tension. On the rule that only evidence records weigh, a pointer to an unretrieved paper does not support the claim it points to, and C009 is now unresolved on the same footing as the other caption-anchored object claims (C012, C044, C015, C059). All other verdicts are held with full treatments; C056's grade is kept but its reasoning now says plainly that its support is indirect (E013 and E016 cover two of the three classes; nothing covers sacred centres). The article keeps the incumbent's structure and all twelve plates, rewrites the Jiroft paragraph to match the corrected grade, removes a reference to a statue study that is in the founding input but not in the ledger, and sharpens the opening statement of how thin the ground is so a reader understands what a self-report is before meeting the numbers. The featured set is unchanged because it already maps the controversy: the thesis-side signal (C027), the strongest null (C057), the base rates (C005, C025, C056), each competing account's mechanism (C034 retelling, C047 convergence, C035 the lost-civilisation bound, C026 the limit on catalogue maps), and the dated and functional rungs each parallel stands on (C059, C012, C044, C009, C018, C015, C028, C053). Catalogued children (C016, C019, C043, C045, C046, C048, C055, C058, C060–C064, C066, C003, C010, C021, C023, C049–C051, C036) stay under their parents and are spanned in the article where they help. Research order is held: the blind human lineup (R003) is the only test that can move the one positive signal; the navel source histories (R002) can dissolve or confirm a whole theme by desk work; the handled-object primaries (R001) replace captions with excavators' and wear analysts' statements.
article:
## The pattern people see

Set the pictures out in a row and the resemblance does its work before anyone has made an argument. An eagle-headed figure strides across a palace wall from Nimrud with a bucket in one hand and a cone in the other. A vulture spreads its wings on a Neolithic pillar at Göbekli Tepe, and along the pillar's top edge sit three arched shapes with handles. A seated man on an Olmec boulder from La Venta holds a small bag inside the coils of a crested serpent. Two bird-headed men face one another on the back of a statue taken from Rapa Nui. A netted stone at Delphi marks the navel of the world; so, in their own languages, do places in the Andes and the Pacific. A teacher comes from the sea, brings the arts, and leaves. A flood drowns everyone but a few.

{plate:IMG-DEEP-P01}

The eye reads these as kin. The question this case asks is whether history does — and, just as much, how one could tell. The founder's Deep Memory pages put the question without answering it: how much of the resemblance belongs to a shared past, and how much to the ways people make images, tell stories and look for connections? Their working rule is that [the historical meaning of a visual resemblance depends on the objects' dates, contexts, differences and possible connections, not on the resemblance alone]{claim=DEEP-C002}. Everything below is an attempt to apply that rule to a ledger that is, so far, almost empty.

### How thin the ground is

A reader should know before going further what this case has to weigh. Every evidence record in the ledger comes from one source: the founder's own home page, a self-published web essay that describes itself as AI-assisted and reports five investigations its author ran. The method calls this a *self-report* — an author's statement of an unaudited result, with the data and the code not in hand — and admits it as weak support at most. None of the primary literature the page leans on is yet in the ledger: not the wear-trace study of the Jiroft object, not the excavators' discussion of Pillar 43, not the published study of the Rapa Nui statue in the British Museum, not the fragments of Berossus, not a single ritual text or chronicle. So nothing here is graded above “weakly supported”, and most of the claims that matter are graded “unresolved”: they stand in the catalogue, anchored to the page that made them, with no evidence record for or against. That is not a finding that they are false. It is a finding that they are untested, together with a list of what would test them.

## Four accounts, set side by side

The founding pages name four explanations and insist that more than one can be true in different cases. This edition treats them as the live accounts.

- **A common source.** The forms and stories descend from one ancestor and were carried outward. In its strongest version — the lost-civilisation account — that ancestor is an unknown society of great age and capability whose emissaries taught the rest. It predicts that the specific composites (this pose with this object in this arrangement; this arrival, teaching and departure in this order) recur more often than chance across the compared cultures, and that the oldest examples cluster near the source.
- **Long-distance contact.** Particular cultures met and exchanged images or stories, with no single ancestor. It predicts dated intermediates and a plausible route, and resemblance strongest where the route runs.
- **Independent invention, or convergence.** Similar bodies, animals, materials and practical problems make similar forms; similar experiences of disaster make similar stories. It predicts that the broad classes are common everywhere, that a handle or a folded hand appears wherever carvers face the same problem, and that the specific composites do not travel together more than comparison bundles do.
- **Later retelling.** Much of the resemblance is made after the fact: by translation, by borrowing between cultures after contact, by comparative writers who smooth different stories into one biography, and by the selection of matching examples from a very large pool. It predicts that similarity grows between an original account and its modern summary, and that details associated with a famous version turn up unevenly, where that version was preached.

The rest of this article takes the themes in turn, asks what the ledger holds for each account, and names the observation that would decide between them.

## Bird-men

{plate:IMG-DEEP-P10}

The gallery of bird-headed figures runs from the shaft scene at Lascaux — a stick-figure man with a bird's head falling beside a wounded bison, a bird on a staff nearby — through Egyptian gods and Assyrian genii to costumed dancers in the Americas and the birdman cult of Rapa Nui. The founding pages themselves supply the first objection: [the description “bird-man” groups at least three distinct ideas — a deity with a bird's head, a person wearing feathers, and a person transforming into a bird]{claim=DEEP-C004}. If the compared images fall into different ones of these, the parallel is not one resemblance but three weaker ones. This edition grades that distinction as provisionally supported on priors — the gallery plainly spans all three — while noting that no evidence record has yet sorted the compared images.

{plate:IMG-DEEP-P05}

The Rapa Nui example is where dates bite. Hoa Hakananai'a, the basalt moai taken from Orongo and now in the British Museum, carries on its back two facing birdmen, a ring and girdle, komari and paddles. The claim that matters most is that [the birdman carvings on the back were added later than the statue's manufacture]{claim=DEEP-C059}, itself placed at around 1000–1200 CE. If so, the Rapa Nui leg of the bird-man comparison is not only an ocean away from Lascaux and Nimrud but some sixteen millennia later than the one and two millennia later than the other — and centuries later than the statue it decorates. The ledger holds no evidence record for this: the published study of the statue that the page cites has not been read. The claim is unresolved.

The catalogue experiment gives the other half of the picture. It reports that [a broad bird-person motif class occurs in 55% of 926 sampled traditions]{claim=DEEP-C005}. A *base rate* is the frequency of a thing in the population at large; a motif found in more than half of all sampled traditions is one you would expect to meet in any two cultures picked at random. That number, if it holds, is the single strongest reason in the ledger not to be surprised by a bird-man in two places. But the page qualifies its own figure twice, and the ledger records both qualifications: the catalogue's coverage is uneven, particularly for the ancient Near East and Rapa Nui — the very regions compared — and broad narrative categories are not the specific images or place names in the claim. A class that includes every winged soul and feathered dancer does not tell you how often a profile head, a bent limb and a rounded form nearby occur together. That composite, not the class, is the thing a common-source account needs, and no one has yet counted it.

## The handled objects

{plate:IMG-DEEP-P02}

Four objects make the comparison: the three arched forms on Pillar 43, the bucket carried by the Assyrian genii, the carved chlorite objects from the Halil Rud valley in Iran, and the small pouch held by the seated figure on Monument 19 at La Venta. Their outlines rhyme; the founding pages say so, and this edition agrees that they are worth looking at closely. Then the pages make the distinction the whole theme turns on: [shape and function are separate questions]{claim=DEEP-C065}.

The four are not on the same footing. For the Assyrian object, [ritual context supports a bucket-and-purifier interpretation]{claim=DEEP-C044}; the *banduddû* is [named in ritual texts]{claim=DEEP-C043}, and the cone in the genie's other hand is what sprinkles from it. For the Göbekli forms, [the function remains uncertain]{claim=DEEP-C012}: no secure identification has been published. The comparison, in other words, sets a known bucket beside three shapes whose purpose no one knows. If the Göbekli forms turned out to be containers, the resemblance would gain a rung; if they turned out to be something with no handle at all, it would lose one. Neither the Assyrian texts nor the excavators' discussion has been retrieved for this ledger, and both claims are unresolved.

{plate:IMG-DEEP-P04}

The Jiroft object is the one case where function has reportedly been tested physically. The page's caption says the chlorite “handbag” in the National Museum of Iran [shows wear on its handle consistent with having hung on a cord]{claim=DEEP-C009}, and points to a published wear-trace study by Vidale and Micheli for it. What the ledger holds is the pointer, not the study: a record that the page cites a paper whose title says it infers the object's function from its wear traces. That is *context* — it tells us where the evidence is — and not support, because what the paper found has not been read. The claim is unresolved. Retrieving the study is desk work, and it leads the third item of the research programme.

{plate:IMG-DEEP-P03}

At La Venta, the figure's pouch is [usually read as an incense bag]{claim=DEEP-C010}, and the serpent that frames him is [often called the earliest known feathered serpent]{claim=DEEP-C003}. Neither reading has an evidence record yet.

What would move this theme? A handle is a practical solution that can recur wherever people carry things. What a common-source account needs, and what convergence does not predict, is that the *particular* handle — its attachment, its proportion to the body, its decoration, the figures beside it — recurs more often across the compared objects than across a control set of handled containers from cultures known to be unconnected. No one has run that comparison.

## Pigs, lizards and other stone animals

The animal comparisons extend the same logic. A low body, a raised back and a projecting snout make a boar legible across any distance; splayed limbs and open jaws make a crouching predator. Here the ledger holds one narrow observation: the Göbekli Tepe excavation team's discussion of Enclosure C [distinguishes boars from snarling predators]{claim=DEEP-C045} — that is, the people who dug the site read the animals in their setting, as an arrangement, not as isolated silhouettes. The founding pages are right that “lizard” should stay a proposed identification where the animal is uncertain, and that the next useful comparison is with other securely identified pig and boar sculptures rather than with whatever looks alike. Nothing in this theme is graded; it awaits objects with museum numbers.

## The navel of the world

{plate:IMG-DEEP-P06}

The linguistic parallel is the most evocative and, on inspection, the most fragile. Delphi's *omphalos* — the netted stone said to mark where Zeus's eagles met — is Greek and ancient. Cusco is glossed as the navel of the Inca world in Garcilaso's account, written after the conquest. Rapa Nui is Te Pito o te Henua, and a smooth stone near Ahu Te Pito Kura carries a name [glossed as “navel of light”]{claim=DEEP-C019}. Göbekli Tepe means “navel hill” in Turkish.

The founding pages' own claim is the crux: [these are different kinds of evidence, differing in language, date of first record and whether the ancient builders used the name]{claim=DEEP-C018}. This edition grades it provisionally supported on priors — Greek, Spanish, Rapanui and Turkish are four languages, recorded across some two and a half millennia — while noting that none of the four source histories has been retrieved. The sharpest test is the Turkish name. If [the modern Turkish name Göbekli Tepe describes the shape of the mound]{claim=DEEP-C015}, it is a descriptive toponym given long after the builders were gone and says nothing about what they believed. The page states exactly this, and adds that [the Kurdish names for the site mean “wish hill”]{claim=DEEP-C016}; but the ledger's one evidence record on the site's names covers the Kurdish gloss, not the Turkish, and neither is sourced on the page. The claim is unresolved, and the second item of the research order is to trace all four names to their first attestation.

What would change the picture: an early, builder-attested “navel” usage at two or more of the sites. What would settle it the other way: source histories showing, as the page proposes, that one name is a modern description, one a colonial gloss, and only Delphi's an ancient sacred designation in the language of the people who used it. A shared bodily metaphor for a centre is possible in any language; a particular inherited usage would need more than this.

## Hands on the belly

{plate:IMG-DEEP-P07}

The hands are part of what makes the monuments feel related. [Arms and hands are carved on the central T-pillars of Enclosure D at Göbekli Tepe]{claim=DEEP-C023}; the shaft is a body and the T a stylised head. Urfa Man, a life-size limestone statue from Şanlıurfa of about 9000 BCE with dark inlaid eyes, [holds its hands over the genitals]{claim=DEEP-C021}. The moai of Ahu Tongariki, carved some ten millennia later, meet their hands low on the abdomen above the belt. The Ponce monolith at Tiwanaku [holds its hands to the chest]{claim=DEEP-C050}, one of them around [a snuff tablet]{claim=DEEP-C051}.

{plate:IMG-DEEP-P08}

The founding pages make the observation the eye tends to skip: a hand across the abdomen and a hand at the groin are close in outline but different observations. And they offer the convergence account in its plainest form. [Carving limbs against a stone body can protect them from breakage]{claim=DEEP-C046}, so [material constraints are a plausible contributor to the hands-on-body pose]{claim=DEEP-C047}. This edition grades that provisionally supported on priors: any carver of a monolith knows what happens to a free-standing arm. The pages are equally right that [material constraint as a contributor to the pose does not settle its symbolic meaning]{claim=DEEP-C048} — a constraint explains why hands rest against the body, not why they rest at the abdomen rather than the groin or the chest. The observation that would decide between constraint and descent is a survey of stone figures in the same media from cultures with no possible connection: if the pose varies with the stone and the tool, constraint wins; if it clusters along a route, something else is happening.

## Serpents, and the feathered serpent

{plate:IMG-DEEP-P12}

Snakes are everywhere in the gallery: coiled around the Olmec figure at La Venta, gripped by the hero on the Jiroft object, projecting in feathered collars from the Temple of the Feathered Serpent at Teotihuacan. The catalogue experiment reports [a broad cosmic-serpent motif class in 37% of sampled traditions]{claim=DEEP-C025} — another high base rate, graded weakly supported on the same self-reported footing as the bird-men figure. The feathered serpent of Mesoamerica is a much more specific thing than “snake”, and any comparison worth making has to preserve the feathers, the head, the body's arrangement and its relation to a human figure.

The page adds the methodological point that governs both catalogue results: [a catalogue's geographical distribution of a broad motif class cannot by itself distinguish independent invention from very old transmission]{claim=DEEP-C026}. The same map is compatible with a serpent invented a hundred times and a serpent inherited once. Distinguishing them takes dated intermediates or a model with stated assumptions — neither of which the ledger yet holds.

Taken together, the catalogue experiment's headline is the most consequential thing in the case and the least tested. It reports that [the three broad motif classes — birds, serpents, sacred centres — are each widespread]{claim=DEEP-C056}, and that [their bundle does not stand out against the study's documentation-preserving comparisons]{claim=DEEP-C057}. If the second holds, then finding birds, serpents and a sacred centre together in a tradition is no rarer than finding any comparable trio of common motifs — which is what convergence predicts and a common source does not. But the ledger contains no evidence record supporting that finding, only the page's two qualifications of it; and even the first claim is supported only indirectly, through the bird and serpent figures, with no number recorded for sacred centres at all. The bundle claim is graded unresolved, and it is the claim whose data this edition would most like to see.

## The people who brought the arts

{plate:IMG-DEEP-P09}

The narrative parallel is as arresting as the visual one. A figure arrives, often from the sea; teaches writing, agriculture, law or craft; changes human life; departs, sometimes promising to return. Oannes in Babylonia, Viracocha in the Andes, Quetzalcoatl in Mexico and Bochica among the Muisca recur in the comparison. The founding pages' caution is that the exact arrival, teaching and departure have to be read in each account, not supplied by a composite biography.

One of the figures has a dated image behind him. On a basalt basin from Assur, the god Ea stands with streams flowing from him beside a fish-cloaked sage; the page holds that [this fish-cloaked figure is the apkallu type the texts actually name]{claim=DEEP-C052}, and that [Berossus's Oannes corresponds to it]{claim=DEEP-C053}. Oannes is thus the one civiliser with a documented iconographic type — but Berossus survives only in later excerpts, and neither the excerpts nor the apkallu texts have been read for this ledger. Unresolved.

{plate:IMG-DEEP-P11}

At Tiwanaku, the staff-bearing figure with the rayed head in the central register of the Gate of the Sun is often called Viracocha. The page's claim is that [that identification is a modern one]{claim=DEEP-C028}. If so, the most-reproduced “image of Viracocha” is not evidence that the story existed before the Spanish wrote it down. Unresolved, for want of a record.

The one measured result in this theme is the founder's V1 lineup experiment. AI judges were shown a civiliser account and asked to pick its partner from a lineup; [the claimed partner ranked first in 62.5% of completed lineups, against 9% for random pairs]{claim=DEEP-C027}. That is a real signal under the experiment's conditions, and the only evidence record in the ledger that points toward a resemblance beyond base rates. It is also, on the page's own statement, badly confounded: the lineups were recognisable, and they used compressed modern accounts. A model that has read the comparative literature knows that Viracocha and Quetzalcoatl are supposed to match. And a lineup of modern summaries measures the similarity of modern summaries. That is exactly the mechanism the retelling account proposes — [stories can become more alike than their originals through translation, borrowing and comparative writing]{claim=DEEP-C034} — and the page's later audit of the original passages has not rerun the test. The decisive experiment leads this edition's research order: rerun the lineup with human raters on unrecognisable passages from the original sources — Berossus via his excerptors, the early Andean chroniclers, Sahagún, Simón — against random hero narratives, and see whether 62.5% survives.

The lost-civilisation account attaches to these figures its strongest claims: that the teachers were emissaries of a real, identifiable, technically advanced society of great age. The page's answer, which this edition adopts on priors, is that [similarity between motifs alone cannot establish a lost-civilisation account's claims about the source's identity, date and capabilities]{claim=DEEP-C035}. A resemblance can at most suggest a connection; who was connected to whom, when, and what they could do, needs evidence of a different kind, and none is in this ledger.

## What survives the water

Flood stories raise several questions at once: whether people remember local disasters, whether particular stories travelled, and whether traditions preserve much older environmental knowledge. The founder's text-coding pilot had an AI code the details of 263 flood-story summaries. It reports that [the coded details cluster by region]{claim=DEEP-C031}, that [details associated with Genesis are unevenly distributed]{claim=DEEP-C054}, and that [generic flood motifs are widespread]{claim=DEEP-C055}.

Each of the four accounts can live with regional clustering: inheritance with regional drift, contact along routes, independent memory of local floods, retelling in regional missions. The uneven distribution of Genesis details is the more pointed finding, because it is what the retelling account predicts — and yet, as the page says, recording a story after contact does not establish that it was borrowed. None of these three claims has an evidence record in the ledger, and the pilot itself coded one compiler's summaries rather than a representative collection of original accounts. All three are unresolved. What would move them: the coded data released and re-coded by human readers against original texts, with the Genesis-associated details dated, where possible, to before or after missionary contact.

## Indus and rongorongo

The companion project compares the sign inventories of two undeciphered scripts and the illustrations used to connect them. Its governing claim is the one this case would apply everywhere: [a visual resemblance between signs of two undeciphered scripts does not establish shared sound, meaning or descent]{claim=DEEP-C036}. Sign shapes converge between scripts known to be unrelated; the ledger holds the principle and none of the companion's results.

## When resemblance becomes evidence

Can the resemblance people see be measured at all? The founder's three image pilots tried to make AI judges rank objects by likeness. The page reports that [judges disagreed strongly with one another about the same objects]{claim=DEEP-C037}, and that [matching the kinds of objects in a lineup changed the lineup result]{claim=DEEP-C038}. The second has an evidence record and is graded weakly supported; the first does not, and is unresolved.

The second finding is the more important. *Diagnosticity* is how much an observation decides between rival explanations. If a lineup that pits a pillar against a moai, a relief and a boulder ranks them one way, and a lineup of pillars against pillars ranks them another, then part of the original resemblance was an artefact of comparing unlike kinds — and that is a finding about every side-by-side gallery, including the one that opens this article.

## Where this leaves the question

The ledger, read strictly, says this. The broad classes — bird-people, cosmic serpents, sacred centres — are common enough that meeting them in two cultures is expected. Whether the specific composites are rarer than chance has not been counted. The one positive signal, the civiliser lineup, is confounded in exactly the way the retelling account predicts. The navel parallel rests on four names whose source histories have not been traced, one of them very probably modern. The dating that would place the Rapa Nui birdmen centuries after their statue, the texts that would make one “handbag” a known bucket, and the wear that would make another a hung container, are asserted but unrecorded.

The verdict of this edition is *unresolved*, and the word is chosen, not defaulted to. It means the featured hypothesis — that the resemblances record a shared past — has neither support nor refutation in the ledger, because the ledger holds one unverified source and no primary text. It does not mean the evidence is balanced. Such evidence as there is leans, weakly and by the founder's own report, toward base rates, convergence and retelling.

What would change our mind, in either direction:

- A blind human lineup of original civiliser passages that beats random pairs by a margin like V1's — or one that does not.
- A count of specific composites (pose plus object plus arrangement; handle attachment plus proportion plus decoration) across the compared objects and a kind-matched control set.
- The four navel names traced to first attestation, with the builders' usage documented or shown absent.
- The excavators' discussion of Pillar 43, the wear-trace study of the Jiroft object and the published study of Hoa Hakananai'a read, and their statements recorded in place of the page's captions.
- Dated intermediates and a route for any one of the parallels.

The best argument for the shared past that this edition does not answer is that the null result of the catalogue experiment, by the page's own admission, tests broad classes rather than the specific images in the claim — so the strongest evidence against a common source has not actually been aimed at it — and that the lineup signal, however confounded, is a measurement, where the critics have so far offered only reasons. Both are fair. Both point to the same thing: the next steps are small, cheap and named, and this case waits on them.

assessment.synthesis: The ledger holds twelve evidence records, all weak, all from one source: the founder's self-published, AI-assisted home page reporting its own unaudited experiments. No primary text — excavation report, wear study, statue study, chronicle, ritual text — has been retrieved, and every object-level claim (the Göbekli forms' function, the Assyrian bucket's textual identification, the Jiroft handle wear, the Rapa Nui carving date, the Turkish toponym, the Viracocha label, the Oannes–apkallu match) rests on a page caption with no record for or against. On that footing the featured hypothesis, that the resemblances record a shared past, can be neither supported nor refuted, and the verdict is unresolved. The word is chosen, not defaulted to: each alternative verdict requires a record the ledger lacks. Such evidence as exists leans toward the conventional accounts. The catalogue experiment reports base rates of 55% (bird-person, DEEP-E013) and 37% (cosmic serpent, DEEP-E016) for broad classes, which make a bird-man or a serpent in two cultures expected rather than surprising, though the page's own qualifiers (DEEP-E018, DEEP-E019) note uneven coverage and that broad classes are not the specific images. Its headline null — the motif bundle does not stand out against comparison bundles (DEEP-C057) — has no supporting record at all. The only record pointing toward resemblance beyond base rates is the V1 civiliser lineup (DEEP-E020, DEEP-E021: 62.5% against 9%), which the page itself confounds with recognisable, compressed modern accounts — exactly the retelling mechanism (DEEP-C034), although that limitation survives only in the founding input, not as a ledger record. The image pilots' one recorded finding (DEEP-E022) is that kind-matched controls change lineup results, a warning about every side-by-side gallery. The single evidence record whose removal would most change the case verdict is DEEP-E020: without it nothing in the ledger points toward a resemblance beyond base rates, and the case would tilt from unresolved toward weakly supported for convergence and retelling.
assessment.steelman: The strongest case for a shared past that this assessment does not answer has two parts. First, the only evidence in the ledger that could count against a common source — the catalogue experiment's finding that the motif bundle does not stand out — tests broad narrative classes, and the page concedes (DEEP-E019) that broad classes are not the specific images or place names in the claim. A composite of profile head, bent limb and rounded form, or of handle attachment, proportion and decoration, has never been counted against a control set; so the null result has not actually been aimed at the hypothesis it is taken to undermine, and the 55% and 37% base rates disarm only the weakest form of the parallel. Second, the V1 lineup produced a measured signal (62.5% first-rank against 9% for random pairs) under stated conditions, and the objections to it — recognisability, compression — are reasons, not measurements; until the blind human rerun is done, the one experiment in the ledger with a result favours the resemblance being real. Neither point changes a verdict, because neither adds a record; both name the test that would.
assessment.whatIsClaimed: That a set of recurring forms and stories — bird-headed figures, small handled objects, hands folded on the body of a stone figure, sacred centres named as a navel, feathered serpents, teachers who arrive, bring the arts and depart, floods that few survive — appear across distant ancient cultures (Göbekli Tepe, Nimrud, Jiroft, La Venta, Delphi, Cusco, Tiwanaku, Rapa Nui) because they descend from a shared past, whether one common source or long-distance contact, rather than arising independently or being assembled after the fact by retelling and comparison.
assessment.whereDisagreementLives: Not in whether the outlines rhyme — everyone agrees they do — but in four places. Whether the broad classes' high base rates dispose of the parallels, or whether the specific composites are rarer than chance (no count exists). Whether the civiliser lineup signal measures the original accounts or the modern summaries that compress them. Whether the four navel names share anything beyond a bodily metaphor, given their different languages, dates and users. And whether resemblance can be measured at all when kind-matched controls change the ranking and AI judges disagree.
assessment.whatWouldSettleIt: For the shared-past account: dated intermediates and a plausible route for any one parallel; a specific composite (pose plus object plus arrangement; handle attachment plus proportion plus decoration) occurring across the compared objects more often than across a kind-matched control set from unconnected cultures; a blind human lineup of original civiliser passages that beats random pairs by a margin like V1's; an early, builder-attested navel usage at two or more sites. Against it: the catalogue's bundle comparison data released and holding under narrower classes; the blind rerun collapsing toward chance; source histories showing the Göbekli name modern and descriptive, the Cusco gloss colonial, the Viracocha identification modern; the Rapa Nui birdmen dated centuries after their statue; the Göbekli handled forms identified as something other than containers.
assessment.bestConventionalExplanation: Broad motif classes are common everywhere — a bird-person in more than half of sampled traditions, a cosmic serpent in more than a third — so meeting them in two cultures is the expectation, not the anomaly. Shared bodies, animals, materials and practical problems produce convergent forms: a handle is how anyone carries a thing, hands against a stone body are how a monolith keeps its arms. The compared set is selected for resemblance from a very large pool of objects, and comparing unlike kinds inflates the likeness that kind-matched controls remove. Stories converge through translation, comparative writing and missionary contact, so compressed modern summaries of Oannes, Viracocha and Quetzalcoatl are more alike than their originals. The navel names are four languages recorded across two and a half millennia, one of them a modern Turkish description of a mound's shape.

components.label: Catalogue base rates and the bundle test (C005, C025, C056, C057)
components.note: The 55% and 37% figures are self-reported (E013, E016) and qualified by the page (E015, E017, E018, E019); the sacred-centre figure and the bundle null have no supporting record. Together they are the case's main reason to expect the broad motifs anywhere, and its least tested headline.

components.label: The civiliser lineup and the retelling mechanism (C027, C034, C028, C053)
components.note: The one positive signal (E020, E021) is a self-report confounded, on the page's own statement, by recognisable and compressed modern accounts — the retelling account's mechanism. The Viracocha and Oannes anchors are unrecorded.

components.label: The objects: handled forms, bird-men, hands (C065, C044, C012, C009, C059, C047, C004)
components.note: Every function, date and identification rests on a page caption; the one record (E023) is a pointer to an unretrieved wear study. The convergence mechanisms (material constraint; three bird-man ideas) are held on priors.

components.label: The four navel names (C018, C015)
components.note: The parallel very probably dissolves into four languages and dates, but no source history has been traced; the one record (E024) covers the Kurdish gloss, not the Turkish.

components.label: The flood text-coding pilot (C031, C054)
components.note: No record survived; regional clustering fits every account, and the uneven Genesis details are what retelling predicts but do not establish borrowing.

components.label: Method: what resemblance can carry (C002, C026, C035, C038, C037)
components.note: The governing rules are held on priors; the one recorded method finding (E022) is that kind-matched controls change lineup results, which cautions against every mixed gallery.

researchPriority.reason: The next tests are cheap, named and decisive for their themes — a blind human lineup on source passages, four toponymic source histories, three primary retrievals — so information gain per unit effort is high; but the featured hypothesis has a low prior, the ledger currently holds nothing that could support it, and the stakes are interpretive rather than practical.

claimAssessments.reasoning: No evidence record bears on this claim; it is anchored to the page's own statement of method. It is graded on priors as the working rule of comparative archaeology — an outline shared by two objects has been given many different histories in the literature, and none has been assigned from the outline alone. Provisional because nothing in the ledger tests it.

treatment.plainLanguage: Two things looking alike tells you something is worth checking; it does not tell you which history produced the likeness until you know when and where each was made and how they differ.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: A rule for weighing evidence rather than evidence: it is compatible with every account and decides none, but it governs how every other claim in the case is read.
treatment.strongestObjection: It can be used as a shield: if no resemblance ever counts until the full context is in hand, no comparison can accumulate weight, and the rule becomes a way of declining to look.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A documented case in which resemblance alone, without dating or context, later proved a reliable predictor of historical connection at a rate well above chance.
A stated model under which the specific composites in this case are so improbable by chance that resemblance alone would carry weight.

claimAssessments.reasoning: The page reports that the three-class bundle does not stand out against its documentation-preserving comparisons, but the ledger holds no record supporting that finding — only the page's two qualifications of it (DEEP-E018 on uneven coverage, DEEP-E019 that broad categories are not the specific images). The comparison design, the number of comparison bundles and the measure are not in hand. Unresolved is the finding: a stated null result with no data behind it in the ledger.

treatment.plainLanguage: Finding birds, serpents and a sacred centre together in one tradition is reported to be no rarer than finding any comparable trio of common motifs.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: If it holds, it is the most direct evidence in the case against a common source at the level the catalogue can see: the motifs do not travel together more than chance. Its reach is capped by DEEP-E019 — broad classes are not the specific images the thesis is about.
treatment.strongestObjection: The null is aimed at the wrong target: a class that counts every winged soul and feathered dancer as a bird-person cannot show whether a profile head, a bent limb and a rounded form recur together, so the bundle test leaves the actual thesis untouched.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: The coded data and comparison bundles released and the null reproduced under an independent re-coding.
The same test run with narrower composite classes (pose plus object plus arrangement) and the bundle then standing out — which would reverse the finding's direction.
A demonstration that the documentation-preserving comparisons were selected so as to guarantee the null.

claimAssessments.reasoning: Two weak records (DEEP-E020, DEEP-E021) report the page's own statement of its V1 result: claimed partners ranked first in 62.5% of completed lineups against 9% for random pairs. This is a self-report of an unaudited AI experiment; the run data are not retrieved, and 'completed lineups' implies incomplete runs the page does not enumerate. The page's own limitation — recognisable lineups, compressed modern accounts — appears in the founding input but did not survive as a ledger record. Weakly supported as the page's report of a number; nothing more.

treatment.plainLanguage: When an AI was shown one civiliser story and asked to pick its supposed partner from a lineup, it picked the claimed partner far more often than chance.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: The only record in the ledger pointing to a resemblance beyond base rates, so it carries the shared-past side of the case; but it measures the similarity of modern summaries by a judge that may already know the pairings, which is what the retelling account predicts (DEEP-C034), so it cannot by itself distinguish original resemblance from manufactured resemblance.
treatment.strongestObjection: A model trained on the comparative literature knows Viracocha and Quetzalcoatl are supposed to match; 62.5% may measure the fame of the comparison rather than the accounts.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A blind human rerun on unrecognisable source-level passages (DEEP-R003) beating random pairs by a comparable margin — which would raise both grade and diagnosticity.
The same rerun collapsing toward chance — which would confirm the retelling account's reading.
The run data released, showing how many lineups were incomplete and why.

claimAssessments.reasoning: No evidence record; graded on priors. That translation, borrowing and comparative writing can make stories more alike than their originals is the ordinary experience of anyone comparing a modern summary with its source, and the page states it as a possibility to be evidenced, not a result. Provisional because the ledger holds no documented retelling showing convergence of detail.

treatment.plainLanguage: Stories get told and retold, and each retelling can sand off differences and add borrowed details, so two modern versions may resemble each other more than the originals did.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: This is the engine of the retelling account; if it operates on the civiliser and flood material, it explains the lineup signal and the uneven Genesis details without any shared past. It does not by itself rule a shared past out.
treatment.strongestObjection: It is a mechanism, not a demonstration: no one has yet shown, for these particular figures, that the original passages are less alike than their summaries.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A source audit showing the earliest attested Oannes, Viracocha, Quetzalcoatl and Bochica passages share the same specific arrival–teaching–departure details as their modern summaries — which would weaken the mechanism's reach here.
Documented retellings in which detail demonstrably converged — which would firm the grade.

claimAssessments.reasoning: No record; on priors. Claims about a source's identity, date and capabilities are claims about a society, which resemblance between motifs cannot address without dated remains, a route or intermediates. Provisional only because it is untested in the ledger; it is close to analytic.

treatment.plainLanguage: Even if two carvings really are connected, the likeness cannot tell you who the connecting people were, when they lived or what they could build.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Bounds the strongest account: it does not refute a lost civilisation, it says the case's material cannot reach one. Decisive against the lost-civilisation account's extra claims; silent on ordinary transmission.
treatment.strongestObjection: A sufficiently specific and improbable composite, recurring at dated sites along a gradient, could in principle triangulate a source's region and date; the claim as worded forecloses that too quickly.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Dated remains of a candidate source society bearing the motifs in question.
A composite so specific that its distribution alone constrains an origin region and date under a stated model.

claimAssessments.reasoning: No record; on priors. A present-day map of where a broad motif occurs is the end state of two different histories — many inventions or one very old spread — and without dated intermediates or a model with stated assumptions the map alone does not choose. The page states it; nothing in the ledger tests it.

treatment.plainLanguage: Knowing where a motif is found today does not tell you whether it was invented many times or inherited once long ago.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: A limit on the catalogue evidence rather than a finding for any account: it caps how much the 55% and 37% base rates can decide either way.
treatment.strongestObjection: Phylogenetic methods applied to motif distributions claim to recover inheritance signal; the claim may understate what a distribution can carry when combined with a model.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A stated model under which the observed distribution is much likelier under one history than the other, with its assumptions defended.
Dated intermediates for any one motif.

claimAssessments.reasoning: The support is indirect: DEEP-E013 (bird-person 55%) and DEEP-E016 (cosmic serpent 37%) establish two of the three classes as widespread by the page's own report; no figure is recorded for sacred centres, and no record cites this claim as support. DEEP-E018 and DEEP-E019 qualify all three. Weakly supported as far as two classes go; the third rests on the page's word alone.

treatment.plainLanguage: Birds, serpents and sacred centres each turn up in a large share of the world's traditions.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: High base rates make finding any one of these in two cultures the expectation, which favours convergence and selection from a large pool; but common classes are compatible with very old spread too (DEEP-C026).
treatment.strongestObjection: The 2016 catalogue's coverage is uneven exactly where the case looks — the ancient Near East and Rapa Nui — so the base rates may be wrong for the regions compared.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: The coded data released with the sacred-centre figure and coverage by region.
Re-coding under narrower classes showing much lower base rates.

claimAssessments.reasoning: DEEP-E013 and DEEP-E014 record the page's report of the figure (55% of 926 sampled traditions) and its use as a baseline; DEEP-E015 qualifies that the figure says nothing about pose, object and arrangement together; DEEP-E018 and DEEP-E019 qualify coverage and class breadth. Self-report of an unaudited coding of the Berezkin–Duvakin catalogue; data and method not retrieved.

treatment.plainLanguage: More than half of the sampled traditions have some kind of bird-person in them, so meeting one in two places is not a surprise.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: A base rate this high disarms the bird-man parallel at the class level; it does not touch the specific composite, which no one has counted.
treatment.strongestObjection: The class is so broad that 55% tells us little about the images actually compared, and coverage is thin for the regions in question.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: The coded data reproducing or failing to reproduce 55%.
A count of the specific composite (profile head, bent limb, rounded form) against a control set.

claimAssessments.reasoning: DEEP-E016 records the page's report of 37%; DEEP-E017, DEEP-E018 and DEEP-E019 qualify its scope, coverage and class breadth. Same footing as DEEP-C005: a self-reported result of an unaudited coding.

treatment.plainLanguage: Roughly a third of sampled traditions carry a cosmic serpent of some sort.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Another high base rate; but 'cosmic serpent' is far broader than the feathered serpent, and the feathered composite is what the Mesoamerican leg turns on.
treatment.strongestObjection: A base rate for a broad class does not bear on whether feathers, head form and relation to a human figure recur.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Coded data released.
A narrower class (plumed or feathered serpent) counted and found rare outside Mesoamerica — or not.

claimAssessments.reasoning: No record; on priors. The gallery the page itself assembles spans a bird-headed god (Horus), feather-costumed dancers (Cahokia, Etowah) and a soul-bird (the ba), so the three ideas are visibly present in the compared set. Provisional because no record sorts the compared images by category.

treatment.plainLanguage: A god with a bird's head, a person dressed as a bird and a person turning into a bird are three different ideas that happen to look alike.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: If the compared images fall into different categories, one striking parallel becomes three weaker ones, which favours convergence over inheritance of a single idea.
treatment.strongestObjection: The categories may be products of later theology; a common ancestral image could have differentiated into all three, so their distinctness does not refute descent.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A sorting of the compared images by a reader of the primary literature showing they fall into one category after all.
Dated intermediates linking two categories along a route.

claimAssessments.reasoning: No evidence record; the page's caption says the statue is c. 1000–1200 CE and the carvings later, and cites a published study of the statue that has not been retrieved.

treatment.plainLanguage: The birdmen on the back of the Easter Island statue in the British Museum were carved some time after the statue itself was made.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Dating bites here: if the birdmen are late, the Rapa Nui leg of the bird-man comparison is not only an ocean away from Lascaux and Nimrud but roughly sixteen and two millennia later respectively, which strains any common source and favours the birdman cult as a local development.
treatment.strongestObjection: A late carving date does not rule out an older local tradition of the image expressed on a newer surface.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: The published study of the statue read and its stratigraphic or stylistic argument recorded.
Evidence for the birdman image on Rapa Nui at a date earlier than the statue.

claimAssessments.reasoning: No record; on priors. That an object's outline and its use are different questions is a methodological commonplace the page states; nothing tests it.

treatment.plainLanguage: Two things can look alike and be for completely different purposes; the shape does not tell you the use.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: A rule for reading the handled objects, not a finding; it keeps the bucket-known and function-unknown items from being silently equated.
treatment.strongestObjection: If shapes converge because of shared function, then shape does carry information about function, and the separation is too clean.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Functional identifications for the Pillar 43 forms that either match or diverge from the Assyrian bucket.

claimAssessments.reasoning: No record; anchored to the page's caption that the banduddû is a bucket named in ritual texts with the cone used to sprinkle from it. The cuneiform ritual texts and the standard iconographic literature are not in the ledger.

treatment.plainLanguage: For the Assyrian object we can say what it was for, because texts describe it: a bucket used with the cone for sprinkling.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: If the Assyrian object is a textually identified bucket, the comparison sets a known container beside Göbekli forms of unknown function; the asymmetry weakens the common-object reading unless the Göbekli forms are shown to be containers too.
treatment.strongestObjection: Ritual texts naming a bucket do not by themselves prove the object in the reliefs is that bucket; the identification is an iconographic inference.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: The ritual texts and the standard iconographic literature retrieved and the identification recorded.
The Göbekli forms independently identified as containers.

claimAssessments.reasoning: No record; the page says the function remains uncertain and cites the excavators' discussion of Pillar 43 and the archaeoastronomy exchange, none retrieved.

treatment.plainLanguage: Nobody has securely identified what the three arched shapes along the top of Pillar 43 were.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: The comparison's most-cited leg rests on shapes of unknown purpose; a container identification would add a rung, a non-container identification would remove one.
treatment.strongestObjection: Uncertainty about function cuts both ways and cannot count against the resemblance in outline, which is what the page compares.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: The excavators' posts on Pillar 43 read and their statement on the forms recorded (DEEP-R001).
A functional identification from the excavation team.

claimAssessments.reasoning: The only record, DEEP-E023, is context: it states that the page points to the Vidale and Micheli wear-trace study, whose title says it infers the object's function from its wear. What the study found is not in the ledger. A pointer to a paper is not the paper; on the rule that only evidence records weigh, the claim is untested.

treatment.plainLanguage: The carved stone bag from Jiroft is said to be worn on its handle the way a thing gets worn when it hangs on a cord.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Would establish that one handled object was a working hung container; that bears on function, and function tells us little about descent, since a hung container is what convergence would also produce.
treatment.strongestObjection: The wear reading, even if the study confirms it, is one object in one museum; it does not generalise to the class of handled objects.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Vidale and Micheli retrieved and its wear findings recorded (DEEP-R001).
The study reporting a different wear pattern or a different function.

claimAssessments.reasoning: No record; on priors. Greek omphalos, a Spanish-language gloss written after the conquest, a Rapanui name and a modern Turkish toponym are four languages recorded across some two and a half millennia; the page states the differences as questions to be answered, and none of the four source histories has been retrieved.

treatment.plainLanguage: The four 'navel' names come from different languages, were written down at very different times, and only some of them were ever used by the people who built the sites.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: If the four differ as proposed, the navel parallel reduces to a shared bodily metaphor for a centre, available in any language, and stops counting for a shared past; if two share an early builder-attested usage, that is unexpected and worth reporting.
treatment.strongestObjection: A shared metaphor across four unrelated languages could itself be the trace of inheritance; difference in date of record is not difference in origin.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Source histories (DEEP-R002) showing an early, builder-attested navel usage at two or more sites.
Source histories confirming one name modern and descriptive, one a colonial gloss, only Delphi ancient and sacred.

claimAssessments.reasoning: No record bears on it; DEEP-E024 covers the Kurdish 'wish hill' gloss (DEEP-C016), not the Turkish name. The page asserts that the Turkish name describes the mound's shape without a source.

treatment.plainLanguage: Göbekli Tepe means 'navel hill' in Turkish because the mound is shaped like a belly, not because anyone thought it a sacred centre.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: The sharpest test of the navel parallel: a descriptive modern toponym given long after the builders says nothing about their beliefs and removes Göbekli Tepe from the navel set entirely.
treatment.strongestObjection: Descriptive and sacred are not exclusive; a mound could be named for its shape and the shape read as a navel for the same bodily reason the ancients used.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Turkish and Kurdish toponymic records or the excavation reports documenting the name's origin.
Any evidence of a pre-modern 'navel' designation at the site.

claimAssessments.reasoning: No record; on priors. Free-standing carved limbs are fragile; carving them against the body is the obvious protection, and the page states this as a plausible contributor. The catalogued sibling (DEEP-C048) rightly adds that this does not settle symbolic meaning.

treatment.plainLanguage: Stone arms break off, so carvers keep hands against the body; that alone could make distant statues share the pose.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: A convergence mechanism for one of the most-cited parallels; it explains hands against the body, not why at the belly rather than the chest or groin.
treatment.strongestObjection: The pose is more specific than constraint requires: hands meeting on the abdomen above a belt at Tongariki, over the genitals at Urfa, to the chest at Tiwanaku are different gestures, so constraint explains less than it seems — and also less alike than the gallery suggests.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A survey of stone figures in the same media from unconnected cultures: pose varying with stone and tool favours constraint; pose clustering along a route does not.

claimAssessments.reasoning: No record; anchored to a caption. Berossus survives only in excerpts (Polyhistor, Eusebius), none retrieved; the apkallu texts are not in the ledger.

treatment.plainLanguage: Oannes, the fish-man teacher in the Babylonian history of Berossus, matches the fish-cloaked sage type carved in Assyrian art.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: If true, Oannes is the one civiliser with a documented ancient iconographic type, giving the Mesopotamian leg a dated image; but a documented Mesopotamian figure says nothing about the Andean or Mesoamerican ones.
treatment.strongestObjection: Berossus wrote in Greek for a Hellenistic audience centuries after the reliefs; the correspondence may be his own synthesis rather than a continuous tradition.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: The Berossus excerpts and the apkallu texts read and compared.

claimAssessments.reasoning: No record; anchored to the page's caption that the identification is modern.

treatment.plainLanguage: Calling the staff-bearing figure on the Gate of the Sun 'Viracocha' is a modern label; no ancient or colonial source names him so.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: If modern, the most-reproduced 'image of Viracocha' cannot show the civiliser story predates the Spanish record, removing a pre-contact anchor from the Andean leg.
treatment.strongestObjection: The absence of a pre-modern name does not show the figure is unrelated to the later Viracocha tradition; iconographic continuity is a separate question from the label.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A pre-modern source naming the figure — or the Tiwanaku literature confirming the label as a modern attribution.

claimAssessments.reasoning: No evidence record survived for the flood pilot's pattern; the page reports regional clustering of coded details from 263 summaries, coded by one AI from one compiler's summaries.

treatment.plainLanguage: When the details of flood stories were coded, stories from the same region tended to share details.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Every account predicts regional clustering — inheritance with drift, contact along routes, local memory, regional missions — so the finding, even if true, decides little.
treatment.strongestObjection: Clustering of a compiler's summaries may reflect the compiler's regional sources and editing rather than the stories.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: The coded data released and re-coded by human readers against original texts.

claimAssessments.reasoning: No record; page report only. Same pilot and footing as DEEP-C031.

treatment.plainLanguage: Details that look like they come from the Genesis flood turn up in some regions much more than others.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Uneven Genesis-associated detail is what missionary borrowing predicts, so the retelling account gains if it holds; but as the page says, recording after contact does not establish borrowing.
treatment.strongestObjection: Unevenness could equally reflect which regions the compiler documented well, or genuine regional inheritance.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Genesis-associated details dated to before or after missionary contact in the regions where they cluster.

claimAssessments.reasoning: DEEP-E022 records the page's report that matching the kinds of objects in a lineup changed the result; self-report, with incomplete runs and cropping constraints noted by the page.

treatment.plainLanguage: When the AI compared like with like — pillars with pillars — the objects it picked as most similar changed.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: A finding about method that bears on every side-by-side gallery: part of the resemblance in a mixed lineup comes from comparing unlike kinds, which favours the selection-and-comparison account.
treatment.strongestObjection: AI judges have not been shown to reproduce human resemblance judgments, so a change in their rankings may say nothing about what people see.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Pilot data released; the effect reproduced with human raters.

claimAssessments.reasoning: No record bears on inter-judge agreement; DEEP-E022's quote concerns kind-matching, not judges. The page reports strong disagreement without statistics.

treatment.plainLanguage: Different AI judges shown the same two objects gave very different answers about how alike they are.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: If resemblance cannot be measured reliably even by the same method, the measured signals in the case are fragile — but this bears on method, not on any account.
treatment.strongestObjection: Disagreement among AI judges says nothing about agreement among human viewers, whose shared impression is the phenomenon.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Inter-judge agreement statistics released.
Human inter-rater agreement measured on the same lineups.
